In brief

Parody. "The fashionable international world attended en masse this afternoon [...] a quiet honeymoon in the Black Forest": in response to John Wyse Nolan's lament that deforestation will soon leave Ireland "As treeless as Portugal," a long paragraph names every kind of tree it can think of. Like the earlier parody that described a state execution as a stirring social event, this piece apes the society columns of contemporary newpapers. The occasion is a beau monde wedding, which Joyce bizarrely presents as a gathering of trees, assigning sylvan names to all the participants, painting their fashionable clothes in vegetal colors, and substituting seeds, nuts, and berries for wedding rice. He weaves his leafy texture from many elements: onomastic revelry, glances at European names and places, catalogues of trees in epic literary works, lewd suggestions of sex and procreation, and a wonderfully kitschy song from the music-hall repertoire.

At more length

Hearing deforestation mentioned, the Citizen rhapsodizes the bygone great trees of the island and recalls a 19th century song about Ireland's natural beauty. To his sentiment, "Save the trees of Ireland," Lenehan offers a sycophantic second: "Europe has its eyes on you." The parody then proceeds to Frenchify John Wyse Nolan into "the chevalier Jean Wyse de Neaulan, grand high chief ranger of the Irish National Foresters," giving him knightly status and an aristocratic "de." The aspiration to French sophistication is felt also in pretentiously italicized newspaper terms (en masse, motif). An Iberian version of Leopold Bloom, the Portuguese "Senhor Enrique Flor" (Henry Flower), plays the organ in the church of "Saint Fiacre in Horto." The Latin epithet means "in the garden," and Fiacre, patron saint of gardeners, was a 7th century Irish monk who emigrated to France. After the wedding, Mr. and Mrs. Wyse Conifer Neaulan head off to the continent to honeymoon in "the Black Forest."

Joyce may have gotten his idea for a gathering of trees from Homer's picture of the Cyclopic islands: "thickly wooded" with "poplars" and "tall pines rising up, / and leafy oaks," and "olive wood" (9.118, 142, 186-7, 320, trans. Wilson). But a likelier source, first noted by Gifford, is Spenser's The Faerie Queene. In the epic poem's first canto Redcrosse and Una take shelter from a storm and wander through a wood. Two long stanzas name the many kinds of trees that surround them: pine, cedar, elm, poplar, oak, aspen, cypress, laurel, fir, willow, yew, birch, sallow, myrrh, beech, ash, olive, plane, holly, maple. Furthering Spenser's allegorical idea that his protagonists are wandering into religious Error, several trees carry possibly unsavory connotations: the proud cedar, the funeral cypress, the weeping fir, "the Maple seldom inward sound." This association of trees with human significations may have prompted Joyce's conceit—though, if so, his allegoresis takes a very different path from Spenser's. He may also have been aware of other epic catalogues of trees, notably Ovid's Metamorphoses (10.90-105) and Chaucer's Parliament of Fowls (176-82), both of which include vines.

In Joyce's catalogue of ladies attending the wedding, whimsical touches abound, a fair number of them off-color. "Mrs Barbara Lovebirch" recalls the book that Bloom scrutinized in Wandering Rocks: "Fair Tyrants by James Lovebirch. Know the kind that is. Had it? Yes." Molly likes S&M novels, and a French author writing under the pseudonym James Lovebirch did produce several, so perhaps Barbara, or her husband, loves birches for what they can do to a backside. "Miss Daphne Bays" combines the beautiful nymph in book 1 of the Metamorphoses with the laurel tree into which Jupiter changes her to save her from being raped. "Mrs Clyde Twelvetrees" was an actual Dubliner—Joyce seizes on the name, which suggests that she is contributing prodigiously to the reforestation project. "Mrs Helen Vinegadding" alludes to Milton's Lycidas, but as Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner observe, the name also insinuates that she is a gossiping gadabout. Another vine, "Miss Virginia Creeper," slinks about the gathering, while "Mrs Liana Forrest" snakes her way through the canopy. "Miss Bee Honeysuckle" appears to be surrounded by a swarm of buzzing attendants, and "Miss Grace Poplar" carries her tall, lithe form with a certain elegance. "Miss Timidity Aspenall" is tremulous (tremuloides to strangers), and "Miss Kitty Dewey-Mosse" harbors some unspeakable longings.

In the style of a bridal feature in a newspaper, the parody carefully notes the presence of all these women and carefully describes the clothing of the bride (tones of green, grey, emerald, and bronze) and the two "maids of honour, Miss Larch Conifer and Miss Spruce Conifer, sisters of the bride" (similar tones, with accents of rose and coral). Only one male other than the groom merits mention: the bride's father, "the M'Conifer of the Glands." Several men in Irish history have carried the epithet "of the glens" (O'Donoghue of the Glens, O'Donnell of the Glens, James MacDonnell, Lord of the Glens), but Joyce's misspelling of the word gives new meaning to the term. "Gland" is an obsolete word for an acorn, derived from the Latin word for acorn, glans. But in present-day English "gland" suggests only a bodily organ that secretes liquids (hormones, sweat, saliva, semen), and "glans" means only the head of the penis (so named because it looks like an acorn). It is hardly possible, then, to read of this progenitor without thinking of what the cones of pines and firs do: spread their seed.

The happy linguistic convergence of glens, glands, acorns, cones, and the fertilizing glans makes clear that Joyce's gathering represents a fantastic solution to the problem voiced by John Wyse Nolan: "Larches, firs, all the trees of the conifer family are going fast." It is a wedding, after all, the purpose of which is to produce offspring. Just before the discussion of deforestation the Citizen has been bemoaning "our missing twenty millions of Irish should be here today instead of four, our lost tribes." All those Irish people killed by famine or lost to emigration have reduced the country to less than half the population it had in the 1830s. The production of lots of babies is called for, and likewise the spread of many seedlings.

To all this—high-society weddings, epic gatherings of trees, European dignitaries, naughty suggestions of sylvan hanky-panky—Joyce adds a response to the Citizen's ballad about vernal nature. When Senhor Flor has played "the prescribed numbers of the nuptial mass," he concludes with "a new and striking arrangement of Woodman, spare that tree." This 1830 poem by American poet George Pope Morris was set to music in 1837 by English pianist, singer, and composer Henry Russell. Its lyrics are as follows:

Woodman, spare that tree!
Touch not a single bough;
In youth it shelter'd me,
And I'll protect it now.
'Twas my forefather's hand,
That placed it near this cot;
There, woodman, let it stand,
Thy axe shall harm it not.
That old familiar tree,
Whose glory and renown
Are spread o'er land and sea,
And wouldst thou hack it down?
Woodman, forbear thy stroke!
Cut not its earthbound ties;
Oh! spare that aged oak
Now towering to the skies!
When but an idle boy,
I sought its grateful shade;
In all their gushing joy,
Here, too, my sisters play'd.
My mother kidded me here;
My father press'd my hand—
Forgive this foolish tear,
But let that old oak stand!
My heartstrings round thee cling,
Close as thy bark, old friend!
Here shall the wild birds sing,
And still thy branches bend.
Old tree! the storms still brave!
And woodman, leave the spot;
While I've a hand to save,
Thy axe shall harm it not.

These "maudlin ecological lyrics," as Zack Bowen calls them (221), can hardly be performed on an organ, but Russell's song was a favorite on 19th century concert stages. No doubt all the assembled tree-people know them by heart.

John Hunt 2026
